New terms

Linear model
A model whose decision boundary is a straight line (or, with more features, a flat surface).
Non-linear model
A model whose boundary can bend, curve or zig-zag to follow the data.

Reminder

Classification
Predicting a category (e.g. orange or lemon, morning lark or night owl) instead of a number.
Classifier
Any model that does classification.
Class
One of the possible categories (e.g. “orange”). Each data point’s correct class is its label.

Part 1 · Review

Logistic regression

  • How is logistic regression fitted?
    • Video: maximum likelihood in logistic regression (from 8:28)
    • Video: maximum likelihood in general
    • Video: ROC curves and AUC
  • Logistic regression is a linear model: it works well when the classes can be separated by a straight line (or flat surface).
  • Its limits with complex, non-linear patterns:
    • It assumes a straight-line relationship between the inputs and the log-odds of the outcome.
    • Its decision boundary is always straight, so it can’t separate classes that need a curved boundary (unless you hand-craft extra features, such as x2x^2x2).
    • So it can miss complex relationships.
  • We may need more flexible models.

New terms

Decision boundary
The line where a classifier switches from predicting one class to the other.
Maximum likelihood
How the coefficients are chosen: pick the values that make the data we actually saw as probable as possible.
Log-odds
ln⁡(p/(1−p))\ln\big(p/(1-p)\big)ln(p/(1−p)): the quantity logistic regression models as a straight line (Lecture 7A).

Part 1 · Review

Linearly vs non-linearly separable

New term

Linearly separable
The classes can be split perfectly by one straight line (or flat surface). If not, they are non-linearly separable.

Part 2

Non-linear models

More flexible boundaries, and the risk that comes with them

Part 2 · Non-linear models

Non-linear models

  • When the pattern in the data isn’t a straight line, we need more flexible models to capture it.
  • Non-linear models, such as random forests and SVMs, can draw curved or stepped decision boundaries, so they capture complicated relationships and often classify more accurately.
  • The catch: the main risk is overfitting.
    • A flexible model can also fit the noise in the training data, and then does worse on new data.
    • This is the bias–variance tradeoff (end of Part 4).

New terms

Overfitting
The model learns the quirks of its training data instead of the general pattern: great on the training data, worse on new data.
Noise
Random variation in data that isn’t part of the real pattern (measurement error, chance).
Generalization
How well a model works on new data it has never seen.

Part 2 · Non-linear models

Straight vs curved decision boundaries

Part 2 · Non-linear models

From logistic regression to random forests and SVMs

  • Both of today’s models build on what logistic regression does:
    • Random forests (RF) combine the votes of many decision trees (an ensemble). Their boundaries are made of straight cuts, so together they can follow almost any shape.
    • Support vector machines (SVM) look for the boundary that leaves the widest gap between the classes. A basic SVM draws a straight boundary like logistic regression; the kernel trick lets it curve.
  • Extra flexibility brings the risk of overfitting, so two habits matter more than before: tuning hyperparameters, and checking performance on held-back data (validation).

New terms

Ensemble
A group of models whose predictions are combined, e.g. by voting.
Hyperparameter
A setting you choose before training (e.g. how many trees), as opposed to the values the model learns from the data.
Validation
Checking a model on data that was held back from training.

Part 3

Decision trees and random forests

Part 3 · Decision trees

Decision trees

  • A decision tree is a simple model for supervised learning. Here we use it to predict a category (it can also predict numbers).
  • It is shaped like an upside-down tree: a root node at the top, branches, internal decision nodes, and leaf nodes at the bottom.
  • Think of a flowchart: each decision node asks a question about one feature, each branch is one answer, and each leaf gives a predicted class.

New terms

Supervised learning
Learning from examples where the correct answer (the label) is known.
Feature
An input variable, e.g. a fruit’s width.
Node / leaf
A box in the tree. A leaf is a box at the bottom that gives the final answer.

Part 3 · Decision trees

Decision trees: making a prediction

  • A tree predicts by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, following the branches down until it reaches a leaf.

Part 3 · Decision trees

Decision trees: your turn

  • A fruit is 4.0 cm wide and 5.5 cm tall. What does the tree predict?
Show the answer

Width > 6.5 cm? No (4.0), so go right.

Height > 6.0 cm? No (5.5), so go right again.

Prediction: orange (the red path in the picture).

Part 3 · Decision trees

Decision trees: the boundary

  • For a numeric feature, each question checks whether the value is above or below a threshold (e.g. “width > 6.5 cm?”).
  • So the decision boundary is made of straight cuts that run parallel to the axes (only vertical and horizontal lines), which chop the data into boxes.

New term

Threshold
The cut-off value in a question such as “width > 6.5 cm?”.

Part 3 · Decision trees

Decision trees: how big should a tree be?

  • Splitting is repeated from the top down (each new region is split again) until all, or most, of the objects in each region belong to one class.
  • The depth of a tree is the number of levels of questions from the root to the deepest leaf.
    • The orange/lemon tree has depth 2: the 1st level splits by width, the 2nd by height.
  • For any training set we could grow a tree with one leaf for every training point. It would be perfect on the training data, but probably wouldn’t generalize to new data (overfitting).
  • So we prefer smaller (shallower) trees.
  • But which feature, and which threshold, is the most useful question to ask at each step?

Part 3 · Decision trees

Choosing a split

  • Consider the following data. Let’s split on width.

Part 3 · Decision trees

Choosing a split: A or B?

  • Recall: each region predicts its majority class (the class with the most points in it).
  • In both A and B, both sides predict orange, because each side has more oranges than lemons. In A, the two lemons on the right are misclassified; in B, one lemon on each side is.
  • So A and B make the same number of mistakes (2 out of 7: the same misclassification rate). Which is the better split?
  • A feels better: its left-hand region is completely certain (all oranges). Can we put a number on this?

Part 3 · Decision trees

Decision trees: entropy

  • How uncertain is a region (leaf)?
    • All examples in one class: low uncertainty (good).
    • Equal numbers of each class: high uncertainty (bad).
  • We use the class proportions in each region, and a measure of uncertainty called entropy, to decide where to split.
  • For two classes, where ppp is the proportion of one class:
entropy=−plog⁡2(p)−(1−p)log⁡2(1−p)\text{entropy} = -p\log_2(p) - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)entropy=−plog2​(p)−(1−p)log2​(1−p)
  • 0 = completely certain (all one class); 1 = most uncertain (a 50/50 mix).
  • The formula may look arbitrary. The idea to remember: higher entropy = more mixed = more uncertain.
Worked example: is A really better than B?

A: left 2 oranges, 0 lemons → entropy 0. Right 3 oranges, 2 lemons (p=0.6p = 0.6p=0.6) → entropy 0.97.
Weighted by size: 27(0)+57(0.97)=0.69\tfrac{2}{7}(0) + \tfrac{5}{7}(0.97) = \mathbf{0.69}72​(0)+75​(0.97)=0.69

B: left 3 oranges, 1 lemon (p=0.75p = 0.75p=0.75) → 0.81. Right 2 oranges, 1 lemon (p≈0.67p \approx 0.67p≈0.67) → 0.92.
Weighted: 47(0.81)+37(0.92)=0.86\tfrac{4}{7}(0.81) + \tfrac{3}{7}(0.92) = \mathbf{0.86}74​(0.81)+73​(0.92)=0.86

A leaves less uncertainty (0.69 < 0.86), so the tree picks A. The drop in entropy from a split is called its information gain.

New terms

Entropy
A number measuring how mixed (uncertain) a group is.
log⁡2\log_2log2​
“Log base 2”: the power you raise 2 to, to get a number. log⁡2(8)=3\log_2(8) = 3log2​(8)=3 because 23=82^3 = 823=8.
Proportion ppp
The fraction of a group in one class, e.g. 3 oranges out of 5 → p=0.6p = 0.6p=0.6.

Part 3 · Random forests

Random forests

  • Instead of relying on one decision tree, a random forest is an ensemble of many trees.
  • Each tree is trained on a different random sample of the training data (a bootstrap sample), and at each split it only looks at a random subset of the features. This makes the trees different from each other.
  • Each tree makes its own prediction; the forest combines them: a majority vote for classification (an average when predicting numbers).
  • More on random forests: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J4Wdy0Wc_xQ

New terms

Bootstrap sample
A random sample of the same size as the data, drawn with replacement: some rows appear more than once, others not at all.
Majority vote
The final answer is the class that most trees predicted.

Part 3 · Random forests

Random forests: how the vote works

Part 3 · Random forests

Why use many trees?

  • Trees are built greedily: at each node they take the best split for that moment and never reconsider it. There is no going back: once a split is made it is permanent, even if a different early choice would have led to a better tree overall.
  • A single tree therefore easily ends up too complex, and it overfits.
  • A forest averages many different trees, which smooths out the mistakes of individual trees: less overfitting, and more stable, reliable predictions.

New term

Greedy method
One that takes the best-looking step each time, without looking ahead to see where that leads.

Part 3 · Random forests

Why are trees built this way?

Why greedy?

  • Fast: checking every possible combination of splits would take an impossibly long time
  • Simple to build and to understand
  • Still gives good results in practice

The downside

  • Can get stuck with a tree that is good, but not the best (a local optimum)
  • Might miss better overall tree structures
  • The first few splits strongly shape the whole tree

New term

Local optimum
A solution that beats all the nearby alternatives, but not necessarily the best one overall. Like reaching a hilltop in fog that isn’t the highest peak.

Part 3 · Random forests

Workarounds

  1. Pruning: after the tree is grown, cut off branches that don’t improve performance on validation data.
  2. Ensemble methods, such as random forests: many trees built with different random choices, combined by vote.

Note

Some research explores non-greedy ways to build trees, but they need far more computing time.

New term

Pruning
Trimming a grown tree back to make it simpler, like pruning a real tree.

Part 3 · Random forests

Random forests: example

  • Scenario: use a random forest to predict gender (male/female) from two input features, body fat percentage and exercise hours per week.
    • This is binary classification (two classes).
    • Male and female are the class labels.
  • As in Lecture 7A, we split the data into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%).

New terms

Binary classification
Classification with exactly two classes.
Training set
The data the model learns from.
Test set
Data kept aside until the end, to check how well the model works on data it hasn’t seen.

Part 3 · Random forests

Random forests: example in Python

  • RandomForestClassifier() from scikit-learn builds the random forest.
  • We give it the features (exercise_hours_per_week, body_fat_percentage) and the target (gender) separately.
  • n_estimators=500 builds 500 decision trees. More trees make predictions more stable, but after a few hundred the gains are usually tiny and training just gets slower.
  • random_state=2025 fixes the random choices, so you get the same results every time.

Code

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Split the data into training and testing sets
X = data[['exercise_hours_per_week', 'body_fat_percentage']]
y = data['gender']
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=2025)

# Create and train the Random Forest model
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=2025)
rf_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

Output

RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=2025)

Note

data is the table loaded in this lecture’s Colab notebook.

Next, rf_model.score(X_test, y_test) gives the accuracy on the test set: the share of test people classified correctly.

Part 4

Support vector machines (SVM)

Choosing the boundary that leaves the widest gap

Part 4 · SVMs

Overview of SVMs

  • In logistic regression, a straight decision boundary separates the classes. With more than two features, this boundary is a flat surface called a hyperplane.
  • Usually many different lines could separate the same two classes. An SVM picks the one with the widest margin: the biggest gap between the line and the nearest points of each class.
  • When no straight line can separate the classes, SVMs have two extra tools: a soft margin (allow a few mistakes) and the kernel trick (curved boundaries).
  • SVMs are supervised learning methods for classification (and regression). They work well with complex data that has many features.
  • Good visualization: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=efR1C6CvhmE&t=9s

New terms

Hyperplane
A flat boundary: a line when there are 2 features, a flat plane with 3, and the same idea with more.
Margin
The empty gap on either side of the boundary, up to the nearest points.
Feature space
The “map” you get by plotting each data point using its features as coordinates.

Part 4 · SVMs

Margin and support vectors

  • The points closest to the boundary, on the edges of the margin, are the support vectors. They are the only points that decide where the boundary goes.
  • Points far from the boundary have no effect: you could move them (without crossing the margin) and the boundary would not change. In logistic regression, by contrast, every point nudges the boundary.
  • A wide margin matters because it helps the model work on new, unseen data.
  • This makes SVMs robust to points far from the boundary. (It doesn’t make them fast: training can still be slow on very large datasets.)

New term

Support vectors
The data points that “hold up” the margin, like the supports under a bridge. (Vector because each data point is a list of feature values.)

Part 4 · SVMs

Many boundaries, one widest margin

Two classes, red and blue. We want a classifier that takes a point’s (x, y) coordinates and outputs a colour. Many straight lines separate the two classes, so which should we pick?

Part 4 · SVMs

The maths of an SVM, in plain words

  • Two classes, labelled +1+1+1 and −1-1−1. Each data point has a list of features x\mathbf{x}x and a label yyy.
  • The boundary is the set of points where
w⋅x+b=0,w⋅x=w1x1+w2x2+…\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b = 0, \qquad \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dotsw⋅x+b=0,w⋅x=w1​x1​+w2​x2​+…
  • Points with w⋅x+b>0\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b > 0w⋅x+b>0 are predicted +1+1+1; points below 0 are predicted −1-1−1. (The same weighted sum as in logistic regression.)
  • w\mathbf{w}w sets the direction (tilt) of the boundary: it points straight across it. bbb shifts the boundary away from the origin.
  • Goal: choose w\mathbf{w}w and bbb to make the margin as wide as possible while classifying every training point correctly. The margin’s width is 2/∥w∥2/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert2/∥w∥, so a wide margin means small weights.

New terms

Vector x\mathbf{x}x, w\mathbf{w}w
A list of numbers, e.g. a point’s features (width, height).
w⋅x\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}w⋅x
“w dot x”: multiply matching entries and add them up. Many books write it wTx\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}wTx.
∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥
The length (size) of w\mathbf{w}w: w12+w22+…\sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2 + \dots}w12​+w22​+…​
Origin
The point where every feature is 0.

Part 4 · SVMs

What if no straight line separates the classes?

  • Hard-margin SVM insists on a perfect split. It struggles with noisy data or outliers, and fails when the classes overlap.
  • Soft-margin SVM allows some points inside the margin, or even on the wrong side, to get a more robust boundary.
  • It balances two costs. With score z=w⋅x+bz = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + bz=w⋅x+b and label y=±1y = \pm 1y=±1:
hinge loss=max⁡(0,  1−y z)penalty=λ∥w∥2\text{hinge loss} = \max(0,\; 1 - y\,z) \qquad \text{penalty} = \lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2hinge loss=max(0,1−yz)penalty=λ∥w∥2
  • Hinge loss is 0 for a point that is on the correct side and outside the margin (y z≥1y\,z \ge 1yz≥1), and grows the further a point strays.
  • The soft-margin SVM minimizes the average hinge loss + penalty: a linear classifier with hinge loss and L2 regularization.
  • In scikit-learn the setting C controls the balance (it works like 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ): a large C allows fewer mistakes but gives a narrower margin.

New terms

Outlier
A data point far from the others.
Hinge loss
A penalty for each point that is misclassified or too close to the boundary.
Regularization
An extra penalty that keeps the weights small, so the model stays simpler. “L2” means the penalty uses squared weights.
λ\lambdaλ (lambda)
A hyperparameter: how strongly to penalize large weights.
max⁡(0,a)\max(0, a)max(0,a)
aaa if aaa is positive, otherwise 0.

Part 4 · SVMs

The bias–variance tradeoff

  • A central issue in all supervised learning.
  • Bias is the error from using a model that is too simple for the real-world pattern. High bias means the model is consistently wrong in the same way. Example: fitting a straight line to a curved pattern. This is underfitting.
  • Variance is how much the model’s predictions would change if you trained it on a different sample of data. High variance means the model is very sensitive to its particular training data: good on the training set, poor on new data. This is overfitting.
  • More complex models usually have lower bias but higher variance. We look for the sweet spot.

New term

Underfitting
The model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does badly even on its training data.

Part 5

From linear models to neural networks

How today’s models fit into one progression

Part 5 · The progression

Summary

  • Machine learning methods can be seen as a series of problem-solving strategies, not separate tricks.
  • Progression: linear regression → logistic regression → support vector machines (SVMs) → random forests → neural networks
  • Why this order?

Because

Each method fixes a real limitation of the one before. Following that chain builds intuition about when to use each tool.

The order is about ideas, not difficulty: today we met random forests before SVMs.

Part 5 · The progression

1. Linear regression → logistic regression (what if a straight line doesn’t fit a yes/no outcome?)

Key points

  • The natural extension of linear regression to classification: the sigmoid turns the straight-line score into a probability
  • Introduces the core ideas of classification: decision boundaries, linear separability, and reading predictions as probabilities
  • A solid, simple baseline to compare other models against

Where it breaks down

Real-world data is often not linearly separable, which creates a genuine need for more flexible models. Classic examples:

  • XOR: one class sits in the top-left and bottom-right corners, the other in the top-right and bottom-left. No single straight line works.
  • Concentric circles: one class forms a ring around the other.

Part 5 · The progression

2. Support vector machines

SVMs address logistic regression’s rigid boundary in two ways: by choosing the straight boundary more carefully, and by letting it curve.

Margin maximization

  • Comes from wanting a robust boundary: not just any boundary that works, but the most reliable one
  • The support vectors are the critical points that decide it
  • A wide margin tends to generalize better. It is a different rule from logistic regression, not always a better one

The kernel trick

  • Works as if the data had extra dimensions, where a flat boundary can separate the classes (without ever computing those new coordinates directly)
  • Example: one class in the middle of a 2D plot, the other around it. Add a 3rd feature, the distance from the centre: now a flat plane separates them. Back in 2D, that plane looks like a circle.

Part 5 · The progression

3. Random forests: simple parts, complex whole

An alternative route: instead of searching for one perfect model, combine many simple ones.

Ensembles

  • The “wisdom of crowds”, applied to machine learning
  • Many weak learners combine into a strong prediction
  • Bias–variance in action: averaging many trees lowers variance

Decision trees

  • Intuitive and easy to draw
  • Built-in feature selection: unhelpful features are rarely chosen for splits
  • Each tree’s prediction is easy to explain

Diversity through randomness

  • Bootstrap samples give each tree different data
  • Random subsets of features give different trees
  • Diversity improves the ensemble as a whole

New term

Weak learner
A simple model that is only somewhat better than guessing on its own, such as one small tree.

Part 5 · The progression

4. Neural networks: a preview

  • Universal function approximators: in theory, a large enough network can approximate almost any pattern, given proper training.
  • Video: But what is a neural network?
  • Neural networks are where the progression from linear to non-linear models naturally leads. More in Lecture 8.

Connections to what you know

  • A single neuron with a sigmoid activation is logistic regression
  • More neurons, and more layers, give more and more complex boundaries

What’s new

  • Hidden layers learn useful combinations of the inputs by themselves, instead of you designing them
  • End-to-end: one model goes from raw input to output, flexible enough for complex patterns

Part 5 · The progression

The unifying framework

Three important themes

Throughout this progression, three key ideas keep coming back:

  1. Decision boundaries: from straight to more and more flexible
  2. Bias–variance tradeoff: balancing simple and complex models
  3. Input → output mapping: the challenge of turning inputs into useful outputs

Developing intuition

Understanding this progression helps you judge:

  • which method fits which kind of problem, and why
  • when to move from a simpler to a more complex method
  • the basic tradeoffs in machine learning
